CP-24.title: The product README documents neither eval nor validate — nor status, team remove, team workflow-update, ls member or ls project
CP-24.ownerFile: none (a Result field, an export, a flag, a verb payload, or a library read)
CP-24.delta: The product README.md documents every non-hidden command path buildProgram registers. Two sections are added — 'Checking a skill' (`validate <path/name>`: deterministic and offline, no model and no network call; invoked by connect, publish and sync's reconcile, and now by the scaffolded workflow's hygiene job; a folder never connected fails on the managed frontmatter fields, so connect it first) and 'Evaluating a skill' (`eval <skill>`: runs locally, never writes the team repository, costs model calls, and with --commit writes one immutable receipt) — each one paragraph that says WHEN the verb is the right one and points at .planning/specs/2026-09-04-eval-engine.md for the rules themselves, restating neither the hygiene checks nor the receipt semantics. The roll-call line also gains `status`, `team remove`, `team workflow-update`, `ls member` and `ls project`. Hidden verbs (readme, guard-push, receipt-check, and the legacy share pointer) stay undocumented. A recursive, backtick-scoped coverage test in src/__tests__/cli.test.ts keeps the list honest, in the same spirit as the source-literal tripwire.

CP-37.title: Three shipped spellings of 'no team on this machine', naming two different routes
CP-37.delta: One route, one spelling. The zero-team message is `getStartedLines` (`src/lib/invocation.ts`) and it names `setup`, per this default: `setup` is the single onboarding entry point for a fresh machine, and `team join` is the explicit second-team flow a first-run user has no reason to reach. `selectTeam`'s zero-team throw and the root help's Get-started block render from that one source, so a verb that fails for want of a team tells the user exactly what `status` does. Nothing else about `selectTeam` changes: the one-team, unknown-`--team` and ambiguous-bare-ref answers are unchanged. `install`'s not-joined message keeps `team join`, because it names a SECOND team on an already-configured machine, which is that flow.

EV-07.title: Hygiene findings as data (ValidateResult carries a count only)
EV-07.delta: Rev 17 (Ajay), §6.0: validate's result carries the findings themselves, not only how many there were — `{ name, findings: number, warnings: number, assessment: HygieneAssessment }`, where `assessment` is the value `inspectHygiene` returned, verbatim and in order, both buckets. The counts are retained so existing callers are unaffected. This is a payload change only: the exit-code gate, the printed lines and the errors-only fail-closed predicate are unchanged, and no caller may re-derive a finding it was not given. It exists so that a surface rendering the §9 tier shows the check that failed or warned, its file and its line, rather than a number — the same values `formatHygieneFindings` and `formatHygieneWarnings` already print, carried as data instead of text. (This bullet still says 'share'; the verb is 'connect' since 0.1.4 — correct it in the same edit.)

EV-08.title: Eval aggregate on the Result / persisted to the local run tree
EV-08.delta: Rev 17 (Ajay), §6.0: eval's result carries the aggregate it printed. `EvalResult` gains `summary: Aggregate` — the same object `aggregate()` returned and `renderReport()` rendered, byte-for-byte, with no recomputation and no additional field. Nothing new is measured: this only stops an already-computed value from being discarded at the process boundary, and it is what makes a run without `--commit` (a `--working` author-loop run in particular, where `--commit` is refused) legible to a library caller without parsing printed text or re-aggregating raw rows — the latter being the derivation §12 forbids. `attribution` is the aggregate's only free text; it is generated from a closed vocabulary and remains subject to §8 redaction at the point it enters a receipt. The committed receipt remains the only shareable artifact and the only thing any surface may show about someone else's run.

EV-13.title: Receipt reader for the UI (latestReceipt(skillId, version) and the run list per version)
EV-13.boards: SkillDetailEvals, SkillDetailEvalsReport, SkillDetailNoReceipt, SkillDetailPartial, SkillCard, Library
EV-13.delta: §12 gains one paragraph after the card table: "The UI obtains receipts through `terum-skills receipt <ref> [--skill-version <tree>] [--runs]`, which prints the latest schema-valid receipt for that version as JSON, or that version's committed run ids. The verb reads the local team clone only — it never fetches, never writes and never recomputes — and a receipt whose `skill_id` or `version` disagrees with its path is treated as absent, exactly as the README column already does (§5.4). It is a third reader of the same rule and is deliberately fail-open like the README column, not fail-closed like the publish receipt check (§11): a malformed newest receipt makes the UI show no receipt, while CI still blocks the publish. Where the UI and CI can therefore disagree, CI is authoritative."

MC-11.title: config.json identity fields (name, email, default handle) are drawn as editable; only the login wizard writes them
MC-11.delta: `login --set <key>=<value>` is the field-level write §5.4 has always implied by calling `default_handle` "editable any time". It is the one form of `login` that asks nothing: no gh detection, no identity collection. It accepts exactly three keys — `name` (`display_name`), `email` and `default-handle` — validates each with the schema `configSchema` already uses (non-empty string, `emailSchema`, `handleSchema`), writes through `ConfigStore.update`, which remains the only writer of the file, and prints the new value; repeating the flag sets several keys under one lock. It refuses every other key, including `github`: that value is evidence collected from `gh api user` during identity, not a preference, and the schema's `passthrough` must not become a way to write arbitrary keys. It cannot set `teams.<team>.handle`, which only `team create` and `team join` bind and which is immutable once your people file exists. Changing `name` or `email` changes `metadata.author` on every skill you author at the next `sync`, through the §5.3 managed-author refresh that guard row (a) already admits — and the command prints that consequence before it writes, including the half it does not fix: your committed `people/<handle>.json` keeps the `display_name` and `email` recorded when you joined (only `team create`/`team join` write them), so `ls member <handle>` matches your authored skills against the old pair until a people-file refresh ships. `login` with no `--set` is unchanged.

PF-03.title: Person role chip (platform / design / data / founder)
PF-03.boards: SkillDetail, SkillDetailRailClosed, MarketplacePerson, MarketplacePeople, Share, OnboardingSearch
PF-03.delta: `role` is a short self-declared discipline label (`platform`, `design`, `data`, `web`, `ops`, `founder`, ...), defaulted to `''` and capped at 32 characters, shown beside a person's handle wherever the UI names them. It is written only by its owner, through the `profile` verb under guard row (b), and it is **not an authorization**: repo admin remains the only authority predicate (§6.0 rows c-e, D11), no verb reads `role` to decide anything, and the roster's Admin/Member chip is a separate, host-derived value. An empty role renders as nothing rather than a placeholder, and a person with no people file has no role at all — the roster must render an invited row's discipline as blank, the way it already blanks Joined, Teams and Last seen.

PF-04.title: Project membership (person<->project): member counts, facepiles, per-person project chips
PF-04.boards: MarketplaceProjects, MarketplaceProject, MarketplaceProjectNotInstalled, Marketplace, Share, MarketplacePerson, Marketpl… (cell truncated at 120 chars in §1)
PF-04.delta: `projects` is an array of `team.json` project names, defaulted to `[]`, recording which team projects this person considers themselves on. It is self-declared and written only by its owner, through `profile --project` under guard row (b); the verb validates each name against the `team.json` project registry, reading it from the pre-image tree inside the mutation, so the roster can never show a chip for a project that does not exist. It is deliberately **not** authorization and **not** placement: which skills land where is still decided by `team.json projects[].skills` and by worktree resolution (§5.2 project resolution), and a name that later disappears from the registry is ignored by readers rather than pruned. Project member counts and facepiles are derived across all `people/*.json`, never stored, so `team.json` gains no members array and the §6.0 table is unchanged.

PF-07.title: Edit own profile after join (the committed display_name, and bio)
PF-07.delta: `display_name` and `bio` are set at join and, from this revision, editable afterwards by their owner through one verb: `profile [--name] [--bio] [--role] [--project]` writes `people/<you>.json` via `safeWrite` under guard row (b), which gains the `profile` action. It writes **only** self-describing fields: `email`, `github` and `handle` are refused, because `email` and `github` are the identity evidence the §5.4 reclaim rule matches a second machine against and `handle` is the binding identity itself, immutable once the people file exists — the Account pane's locked handle row already draws that boundary. `profile --name` also refreshes `config.display_name`, because `team join` rewrites the committed `display_name` from config identity on every join and reclaim: without the refresh, a people-file-only rename is silently reverted the next time its owner joins from a second laptop. This closes the defect that a name changed after join reaches every SKILL.md at the next sync but never reaches the roster or the generated README.

PF-09.title: Explicit decline path: no verb writes `declined` without a prior install
PF-09.delta: **`decline <ref>`** — records `<ref>`'s skill ID in your own `people/<you>.json` `declined` list and does nothing else: no placement is touched, no `pending` entry is written, and no local file moves, because a decline suppresses a *future* automatic placement rather than undoing a past one. It exists because `uninstall-skill <ref>` resolves its targets from your `installed` records and the machine-local `placements` ledger, so on a team-endorsed skill you were offered but never installed it resolves zero targets, returns before its write, and is a silent exit-0 no-op — leaving the one case the §5.2 opt-out contract is *for* with no verb. It records under the same predicate the `uninstall-skill` bullet already uses: only a skill an automatic path would otherwise place (team-endorsed global *or* project-list) may be declined, so one field keeps one recording rule; a ref nothing endorses is refused in one line rather than committing a permanent, team-readable refusal of a skill nobody offered. `declined` is scope-free (§5.2), so `decline` takes a skill ref only, never `member` or `project`. It is idempotent (an ID already in the list produces no tree change and therefore no commit) and reversible only the documented way — an explicit `install` of that ID clears the entry (§5.2). Authorization is unchanged: the commit is a `people/<you>.json`-only change and the durable guard action remains `uninstall`, the same action `sync` already uses when its orphan pass records a decline; row (b) of the §6.0 table gains `decline` in its "Permitted on" cell (`b / people/<you>.json / join, install, uninstall-skill, decline, sync`), and no other row, no `team.json` write, and no stamp are involved.

RM-02.title: allowed-tools / grants on the card and the approvals view
RM-02.delta: §6 addition to `ls` and `search`. Each carries, per skill, the normalized `allowed-tools` string and its sha256, alongside the fields it already carries. The value is `allowedTools()`'s output verbatim — the same string `install`'s consent prompt and `publish`'s card print — `none` when the skill declares no tools, and `null` when the declaration is malformed, which is the one case that is never hashed. Nothing new is computed and no printed line changes. The point is the hash: it is the key `config.approvals` is compared against, so a second consumer that re-normalizes a grant list on its own can reach a different digest and show 'approved' for a set the CLI considers unapproved. This carries the CLI's own answer instead.

RM-03.title: Who-installed list per skill (the 'uses' popover names)
RM-03.delta: §6 addition to `ls`. `ls` carries, per skill, the install records that produced its install count: handle, display name, scope and `since`, oldest first. This is a re-projection of the same committed `people/*.json` entries `installCounts` already reads and introduces no new number. The two must not be confused, and D38 is unchanged: the COUNT is how many teammates hold the skill (deduped per person and id), while this LIST has one entry per install RECORD, so a teammate who installed the same skill globally and again into a project appears twice in the list and once in the count. Whether a departed teammate's historical install should still appear beside a live roster is not decided here — that is TJ-13's question, and this field reports what the files say either way.

RM-08.title: Update state as a structured value (update returns void)
RM-08.delta: §6, `update` (rev 11), addition. The package-manager advice `update` prints is exported as a function of this copy's `Launch`, so another surface can show the same command without composing one. The printed output and the exit code are unchanged and remain the byte-for-byte issue-8 R.8 contract. Exporting it is the point rather than a convenience: the advice is keyed on this copy's installation provenance and branches five ways, so any consumer that builds an `npm install` line from a version pair is guessing, and a guess here tells the user to run a command that will not update the copy they are running. A caller that wants the comparison rather than the command already has it — `createReleaseState` and `describeUpdate` are exported — and MUST use those to render a version pair, because `update` itself forces a release probe and writes release state on every invocation.

RM-09.title: Typed decline on Result (cancel is not an error)
RM-09.boards: SkillDetailRemove, SkillDetailRunEval, SkillDetailInstall, MarketplaceProjectInstall, SettingsLeave, SettingsPrune, Shar… (truncated)
RM-09.delta: A verb's failing `Result` gains one optional discriminator, `cancelled?: true`, set only where the failure is a human answering no to a `Prompter.confirm` and nothing observable moved. It is spelled `cancelled`, not `declined`, because `declined` is already the committed suppression list on `people/<handle>.json` (§5.2) and the two appear on the same screens. It changes no CLI behaviour — a cancelled result is still one stderr line and exit code 1 — and exists for the second caller §3 already names: the phase-2 UI must tell 'you pressed Cancel' from 'the operation failed' without matching on error prose, which the `share`->`connect` rename has already shown to be unstable. `lib/result.ts` gains a `cancelled(error, value?)` constructor beside `failure`, and a `CancelledError` so a decline thrown inside a verb's body is re-tagged by that verb's existing top-level catch. `PromptClosedError` is never tagged — a closed channel is a real failure — so the flag is set at the confirm site, not in the catch. The three paths that already model a decline as data are unchanged: `ConnectBatch.declined`, `publish`'s open-endorsement refusal, and `offerHook`'s `'declined'` return; in particular `connect`'s batch failure return (which carries a partial batch) stays untagged, because a batch that also failed for another reason is not a cancellation.

RM-10.title: Export the batched skillTrees reader (ls is O(skills) git spawns)
RM-10.boards: Library, LibraryLight, LibraryLoading, Marketplace, MarketplaceSkills, MarketplaceFull
RM-10.delta: `lib/teamRepo.ts` exports one additional read-only helper, `skillVersions(runner, clone, ref = 'HEAD'): Promise<Map<string, string>>`, which resolves every skill's tree hash from a single `git ls-tree <ref>:skills` — the batched reader `safeWrite` has used internally since §9's generic-git README path — and writes nothing. It differs from `latestTree` in two ways a caller must handle: its failure text is `git ls-tree ...:skills failed: <stderr>` rather than `Could not resolve the latest version of <name>: <stderr>`, and a skill git cannot resolve is simply ABSENT from the map rather than an error naming it. Callers therefore keep the §6 per-skill degradation ruling themselves — one unresolvable folder costs one row's version and one printed line, never the roster or the other rows — and `skillVersions` returns an empty map, never throws, when the ref carries no `skills/` tree. It exists because §3's second caller renders the whole catalogue at once, where one child process per skill is the dominant cost. No verb's behaviour or output changes.

RM-11.title: Packaging for in-process import: src/lib-entry.ts barrel, exports map, declaration: true, tarball CI assertion
RM-11.delta: §3's library-first obligation gains its packaging half. `src/lib-entry.ts` is the package's library entry: a barrel that re-exports `run` from all twenty `commands/<verb>.ts` modules under their verb names, plus the read-model and seam modules — `lib/{auth,community,config,constants,execute,fs,guard,hook,invocation,launch,local-skills,package,placer,prompt,readme,remote,result,runner,schema,skill-source,skills,teamRepo,update,version}.js` and `lib/evals/{hygiene,receipt,results}.js`. It is deliberately not `index.ts`, which installs stream handlers and parses argv on import. `execute.ts` is exported on purpose: it is the documented Result -> stderr/exit-code mapping, i.e. the piece a second caller must be able to SEE in order not to reuse it. `package.json` gains `types` and an `exports` map with `.` -> the barrel, `./cli` -> the bin, and `./package.json`; `tsconfig.build.json` gains `declaration` so the types ship inside the existing `files: ["dist"]`. The CI package job's must-have list gains `dist/lib-entry.js` and `dist/lib-entry.d.ts` so the library entry cannot silently stop shipping, and keeps asserting `dist/index.js`, which `lib/teamRepo.ts`'s push-guard launcher resolves at runtime. Adding `exports` closes deep imports into `dist/` that a consumer can reach today (a package with no `exports` permits every subpath); nothing known consumes them, and this is the deliberate cost of a curated surface. No verb's behaviour changes and nothing in `src/` imports `src/index.ts`, so the barrel introduces no cycle.

RM-18.title: print-only information not on the Result (search partial failures, install exclude warning, interactive sync failure payload)
RM-18.boards: OnboardingError, MarketplaceError, LibraryError, ShareError, InboxError, SettingsSync
RM-18.delta: Every verb's Result carries everything the run learned, on BOTH outcomes. A verb that degrades — one team unreachable, one person file unreadable, one exclude line unwritten — records that on the value it returns and does not rely on print to have carried it, because the phase-2 UI (§3) supplies a Prompter whose print is a channel to a human, not a wire format. Concretely: `sync` attaches its SyncResult on the failure path in EVERY mode, not only `--hook` (the hook discriminant on the value stays accurate, so the bin's hook-notice routing in lib/execute.ts is unaffected); `install`'s InstalledResult gains `notices: string[]`, the placer lines it prints today; and `search` returns `{ hits, warnings }`, where warnings holds the per-team degradations it currently only prints. The two verbs deliberately keep DIFFERENT outcome shapes and the difference is the point: a mixed `search` stays ok:true, because a partial catalogue is a usable answer and §6's exit gate should not fail a run that found skills, whereas a partial `install` is ok:false with its successes on the value, because placements already written are durable state a script must not read as clean. Printed output is unchanged in all three cases — this adds to the value, it moves nothing off the terminal.

RM-19.title: Batch verbs without error isolation (install member / project)
RM-19.delta: `install member <handle>` and `install project <name>` isolate per item, exactly as `sync`'s endorsed batch already does. One skill that cannot be placed — a foreign folder at its target, a busy target lock, a declined tool grant — is reported by name and the batch continues; the Result carries every skill that did place. When at least one item failed the Result is ok:false, so the exit code still tells a script the batch was not clean, and its value carries the successful InstalledResults, because those placements are already durable in `config.placements` and in the people file and must never be reported as not having happened. TWO ERROR CLASSES ARE BATCH-FATAL AND ARE RETHROWN RATHER THAN ISOLATED. `PromptClosedError`: a channel that is gone is not a per-item failure. And a remote-access or safeWrite-exhaustion failure: safeWrite retries with backoff to a 30-second deadline before throwing, so isolating it would turn one unreachable remote into one retry-to-deadline loop per remaining item — eight of them behind the drawn 'Install 8 skills' button. A CONSEQUENCE THE IMPLEMENTER MUST EXPECT: an isolated batch can leave one `config.pending` entry per failed item, where today a single throw leaves one. That is correct and not a leak — pending is written before placement and cleared only after the people-file write, sync replays pending, and a team with any pending entry is deliberately left unstamped so the next session retries — but it means an isolated batch changes what the next `sync --hook` does, and that is intended.

RM-21.title: Windows home derivation (placementHome checks a POSIX suffix)
RM-21.delta: The global placement root is derived from the store root with path primitives, never by matching a POSIX separator. `placementHome` walks up from `<root>` only when its last two segments are literally `.terum` and `skills`, using `basename` and `dirname`, which are separator-correct on every platform — the same reason `join` at the agent-paths table is correct. This replaces a suffix test, `store.root.endsWith('/.terum/skills')`, that could never match on Windows, where the default root is `C:\Users\<name>\.terum\skills`: the test fell through, the store root itself was used as the home, and every global placement landed at `<store root>\.claude\skills`, a directory Claude Code never reads. Behaviour on POSIX is unchanged for every root shape the suite already pins. Nothing is stored and nothing is derived from this process's HOME — re-resolving a global path from the environment is the failure §7's orphan pass already refuses.

RM-22.title: Zero-team state and missing-tool detection (git, gh, claude) as first-class data
RM-22.boards: OnboardingBoot, OnboardingError, SettingsAccount, SettingsEvals, LibraryEmpty, MarketplaceNoResults, ShareEmpty, InboxEm… (truncated)
RM-22.delta: Setup and the phase-2 UI can ask, before any question, whether the two tools the product shells out to are present. `gh` is already answerable through the exported `ghState` (installed / authenticated). `git` gains the same treatment: an exported `gitState` that runs `git --version` through the injected Runner and reports installed, returning false rather than throwing on a spawn error. It is a read-only probe — it starts nothing, writes nothing, is not a verb, and is not a readiness test for anything else — and it exists so that a missing binary is a first-class state with its own copy, instead of a raw `spawn git ENOENT` surfacing through an unrelated verb's failure string. The zero-team state needs no addition: `status` already returns ok:true with an empty teams list on a machine that has joined nothing, and a missing config.json reads as an empty config rather than an error.

RM-30.title: No verb payload carries a skill's description, which every card draws
RM-30.boards: Library, Marketplace, MarketplaceProject, MarketplacePerson, SkillDetail, Inbox
RM-30.delta: `ls` and `search` return each skill's SKILL.md `description` on the Result. It is the value both verbs already read — `search` matches on it and `ls` parses the frontmatter it comes from — and it is returned verbatim, unclipped and untruncated, exactly as the README generator returns it. The printed `ls` format line is unchanged: description is a payload field, not a column, because a one-line-per-skill listing cannot carry it without wrapping.

RM-32.title: sync takes no --team, so the per-team 'Sync now' button on the team row has no verb
RM-32.delta: `sync [--team <name>]` restricts the run to one configured team, selected by the same `selectTeam` rule every other team-scoped verb uses; unknown names fail before any work. Every other configured team is treated exactly as a skipped team is: not locked, not fetched, not reconciled, its placements and connected sources untouched, its orphaned placements neither adopted nor declined, and its stamp unchanged — so a per-team sync neither suppresses nor accelerates the session hook for any other team, and no people file outside the selected team is written. `--team` is refused with `--prune`, which is machine-wide, and with `--hook`, which exists to cover every configured team at session start. Exit codes and the skipped-team failure line are unchanged and are computed over the selected team alone; a team excluded by `--team` is not a skipped team for that count.

RM-38.title: 'Recently updated' sort has no field: nothing in the read model carries a last-changed date
RM-38.boards: Library, LibraryNoResults, LibraryLight, LibraryCollapsed, MarketplaceFilters, MarketplaceFull, MarketplaceProject
RM-38.delta: `ls` and `search` each carry one more field per skill, `updated`: the committer date of the most recent commit that touched `skills/<name>`, read with `git log -1 --format=%cI -- skills/<name>` in the team clone and rendered as an ISO-8601 instant. Both readers gain it together because they print through one function (src/commands/ls.ts:84, whose comment already records that search prints hits through it), so the §6 `ls` line format gains exactly one segment for both. It is read-only, taken from committed history, and identical on every clone at the same commit. Like `latest`, one folder git cannot resolve costs exactly that row: the failure is caught, one line is printed, the field becomes an em dash, and every other row survives. This is the tool's first `git log`; §7's 'never a commit or a history walk' governs `resolveVersion` — which resolves a version to a tree — and is not weakened by a read-only date on the inventory. `updated` is the field a UI sorts 'recently updated' by; `installed[].since` and `placements[].placed_at` are deliberately NOT substitutes — the first is per-person, the second per-machine, and neither answers 'when did this skill last change'.

RM-39.title: No read-only health classification: update-available / local-changed exist only inside the mutating sync loop
RM-39.boards: SkillCard, Library, LibraryLight, SkillDetail, SkillDetailHovers, InboxAlert
RM-39.delta: `ls --local` carries one more field per row, `health`, so a caller can ask what state a placement is in without running the sync that would change it. It is a pure comparison of three fingerprints — the one on the ledger entry, the one taken from the placed folder, and the one taken from the tree the clone holds now for that skill — and it is one of `ok`, `update-available`, `local-changed`, `both`, `placement-missing`, or `untracked` (a folder with neither a connected source nor a placement, which has no fingerprints to compare). It performs no write, takes no lock and moves nothing: `quarantineDrift` remains the only thing that acts on a local-changed answer, and §6's local-changed / blocked vocabulary is unchanged — this only gives it a read-only reading. Note that this is a genuinely NEW comparison rather than a restatement of sync's: for a placement pinned to a version, sync compares against the materialized pinned tree, so it never asks whether the team's current tree has moved. A clone the row cannot read costs that row's health alone ('unknown'), the way an unresolvable `latestTree` costs one row of `ls`.

RM-44.title: ls --local rows drop the team and flatten status into prose; the Sharing board draws a team column and a state chip
RM-44.delta: `ls --local` additionally returns, per row, the ledger references it already resolved — each `shared` entry's `{id, team}` and the `placement`'s `{id, team, version}` — and, for connected rows, a machine-local `sharedState`: `in-sync` (both digests equal the baseline), `local-edit` (only the source moved), `repo-ahead` (only the repository copy moved), `diverged` (neither equals the baseline, or no baseline is recorded), `not-connected` (no shared entry). The PRINTED OUTPUT IS UNCHANGED: the state sentences remain the contract, and the structured fields exist so a host need not parse them. `sharedState` is the same comparison §5.3's reconciler makes, factored out and read-only — it digests with the existing `canonicalDigest`, and it never writes, never pushes, never quarantines and never touches `config.shared[].baseline`; the reconciler calls it so the two cannot drift, and §5.3's decision procedure is unchanged by the relocation. It reads two folder trees per connected row, which is filesystem work only: `ls --local` remains no git, no network, no prompt, no write. `diverged` is advisory until the user runs `connect --keep-source <id>` or `connect --keep-repo <id>`, which remain the only resolutions; `repo-ahead` is NOT advisory — the next sync overwrites the local source and moves the previous one to quarantine — and a host must render it as a pending destructive action, not as a quieter `in-sync`.

RM-48.title: No read verb returns the last-sync timestamp, and three drawn surfaces print one
RM-48.approver: Ryan (phase-1 spec section 6 / section 8) — the SAME single approval as RM-41 (per OD-4)
RM-48.boards: InboxEmpty, SettingsTeams, SettingsSync, Library, MarketplaceHome, Share, ProjectDetail, PersonDetail
RM-48.delta: See RM-41's spec delta: OD-4 decided `syncedAt` and `pending` together as option (a), one spec change to §6's `status`, so the two rows share ONE paragraph and ONE Ryan approval. The `syncedAt` half reads: "`status` additionally returns, per team, `syncedAt: string | null` — the ISO timestamp of run/<team>.stamp's last modification, or null when no stamp exists — read from the same stat the stale notice already performs and populated BEFORE the clone is described, so a team with an absent, incomplete or foreign clone still reports when it last synced. `stale` is unchanged: it keeps its current placement inside the readable-clone branch and its current meaning, and this addition makes no claim about it. `syncedAt` is reported VERBATIM, including a stamp dated in the future — the skew rule that makes such a stamp not fresh belongs to `stale` and must not silently rewrite the timestamp. The value means 'this team's last FULLY SUCCESSFUL sync': the stamp is written per team only after that team's run completed with no deferred work and no remaining pending entry (§8), so it is not a claim that anything changed, and null does not mean 'never synced' — `team leave` deletes the stamp with the rest of the team's run artifacts, so a rejoined team reads null while being perfectly current. A host renders it as a freshness disclosure, never as a success receipt. `syncedAt` lands on `status` only; `search` continues to report staleness as its existing one-line notice and gains no timestamp."

They are listed as invitations, never as members, and never counted in the roster. The read carries no admin precondition of its own: GitHub decides what a non-admin may see, and a refusal omits the section rather than failing the verb. On a generic-git remote, without `gh`, or offline, the list is absent with the §6.0 host message; the CLI never remembers an invitation between runs.

TJ-11.title: Cancelling a pending invitation is unreachable: team remove needs a people file the invitee does not have
TJ-11.delta: **`invite --cancel <github-login>...` (rev 13).** The same GitHub-only verb also withdraws an invitation it sent: with `--cancel` it lists `repos/{owner}/{repo}/invitations` and DELETEs every invitation whose invitee login matches, printing one line per login — cancelled, or no pending invitation for that login — and it writes nothing to the team repository, in either direction. Withdrawal is the same authority as revocation, so it runs the same host gate `team remove` runs (§6.0): `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo} -q .permissions.admin`, refusing on anything but `true`. On a generic-git remote it fails before any host call exactly as the send path does, because there is no invitation to cancel (§6.0). It is keyed on the GitHub login because that is all a pending invitation has — the invitee has no `people/<handle>.json`, and therefore no handle, no display name and no role, until they join — and that is also why `team remove <handle>` cannot do this job: `team remove` is handle-keyed and resolves its target through `people/<handle>.json` on `origin/main`, failing before any host call when that file is absent. `team remove` is otherwise unchanged and remains the departure path for a member who has joined. `InviteResult` gains `cancelled` and `notPending` alongside `invited` and `already`, so the phase-2 UI (D21) renders the outcome from the `Result` rather than from the printed lines; under `--cancel` the Slack-ready join block is not printed, and neither is the 50-per-day invitation cap, which is a send-path failure.

CP-11.title: Filter facets with no predicate; AND/OR within a group; badge vs footer count
CP-11.delta: A viewer-set filter over a receipt field is permitted and is not a derived statistic. The Verdict facet admits or excludes a skill by its latest receipt's `verdict` for the version on display (§12:481-482); the Net-lift facet applies a floor to `comparisons.*.net_lift` of that same receipt. Neither reorders a list and neither computes a new number: the counts a facet shows are cardinalities of the filtered set, never an average, a rate, or a score. Two constraints follow from §5.4 and are binding on any filtering surface. First, comparability: a lift threshold may only be applied within one (`provenance.model`, `provenance.cc_version`) pair, so the surface either scopes itself to one pair or shows provenance beside the facet and excludes receipts from another pair rather than silently comparing them. Second, no ranking: a filtered list is still ordered by install count (D38), never by the facet's own number. Facets over non-receipt data — install counts, context size, list, category, author, last-updated — are unconstrained by this section.

CP-13.title: 'uninstall-skill project/member' writes declined — the consequence dialog is undrawn

CP-15.title: Marketplace filter defaults (PASS-only, lift ≥ +20 %, installs ≥ 3) shipped off
CP-15.delta: Filtering is not ranking, and the distinction is deliberate. A viewer-chosen filter over a receipt field — verdict, net lift — narrows a list without ordering it, and is permitted: it states a threshold the viewer set, not a claim that one skill beats another, and the reader can see and clear it. What is not permitted is a DEFAULT filter over a receipt field. A default that arrives with PASS pre-selected, or with a net-lift floor already applied, is the product ranking on the viewer's behalf using precisely the numbers our own probe shows do not rank (Spearman rho -0.07 against SkillsBench all-harness and -0.22 against its claude-code column; §1:31 carries the earlier SkillEvaluator figure, rho -0.11). Every receipt-derived facet therefore ships off, the filter control shows a zero badge on first run, and the unfiltered catalog is what a new viewer sees. Facets over non-receipt data — install counts from the people files (D38), context size, last-updated — are subject to the same default-off rule for consistency of the control, but only the receipt-derived ones are load-bearing here.

MC-10.title: Session-start hook toggle: no verb toggles it, an installed entry is never refreshed, and the design contradicts itself

With no argument it prints the command actually found in `~/.claude/settings.json` — read from the file, never from `HOOK_COMMAND` — or reports that no entry is installed. `on` calls `installHook` directly rather than `offerHook`: it does not short-circuit on an existing entry, so it is how a stale hook command is corrected on a machine that has one, and it asks no y/N because a user who asks for the switch has given the consent. (1) `pending`: the `config.pending` entries for that team as `{op, id, scope, version, started}`, read from the same config load as the rest of the block — `version` is the key `install` writes onto the entry and `sync` replays from, so a pinned interrupted install is distinguishable from an unpinned one. (2) `syncedAt: string | null`: the ISO timestamp of `run/<team>.stamp`'s last modification, or null when no stamp exists, from the same stat the stale notice already performs. Both are populated BEFORE the clone is described, so a team with an absent, incomplete or foreign clone still reports work in flight and when it last synced. `stale` is unchanged and keeps its current placement and meaning. This is a Result-only addition: the printed block is unchanged, because the printed contract is what status's tests and the §12 acceptance walk pin. A non-empty `pending` means this machine is mid-operation — an install or uninstall that wrote its intent and has not yet cleared it — and its only remedy is `sync`, which finishes or unwinds the entry (§5.4, 13.25). It is not an error and not a failure of the last command: an entry survives a decline only when it was already present from an earlier interrupted run. The two fields are read together: a team with non-empty `pending` is not stamped (§8), so an old `syncedAt` beside a non-empty `pending` is the honest signal that the last run left work undone, not that sync failed.

RM-45.title: Git-transport access failure is a separate class from the gh sign-in: no probe is permitted and no fix-it button may ship

The app-side rule to record (a frontend rule, no spec change): "The git-transport access failure is a distinct class from the gh sign-in and is the case two of the four drawn `Open settings` buttons actually land in. The app renders `explainGitAccessFailure`'s text as returned — as selectable text with a copy button on the `gh auth setup-git --hostname github.com` line — and does nothing else: it never probes access, never offers to run that command, never writes credential configuration, and ships no Fix-it button; spec:336 forbids all four, and the command rewrites global Git credential config for github.com and its gist host. Settings > Account's `Access to team repos` row stays read-only for the same reason: there is no predicate the CLI is permitted to evaluate, so a live status there would be a claim the product cannot make. On the `sync` path the app must capture the Prompter's print stream, not the failure string: for a non-hook sync the failure payload is undefined and the message says 'See the notices above', so an app that renders the failure string alone renders a sentence pointing at notices it does not have."

RM-47.title: CloneState's four states have no drawn surface, and it is the likeliest cross-window failure
RM-47.approver: none for the CLI; Teddy for the six copy variants
RM-47.delta: None for the CLI. The app-side rule to record: "`TeamStatus.clone` is a five-arm discriminated union and the app renders one full-surface state per arm, never a generic error: `absent`, `incomplete/not-a-repository`, `incomplete/no-team-json`, `incomplete/unverifiable` (the origin probe threw; advise checking git and do NOT advise moving anything), and `foreign` (a clone of a different remote, naming that origin). Each carries status's own repair line as the secondary action. `absent` does NOT mean 'another window left this team': a completed `team leave` deletes the config entry (src/commands/leave.ts:114) and status iterates config.teams (:33), so a left team VANISHES from the payload. The cross-window-leave signal is 'a team that was in the last payload is not in this one', which the app computes by diffing two StatusResults; `absent` means an interrupted leave, a hand-deleted folder, or a restore that skipped it. A SIXTH surface is required beside the five arms: a per-team read failure with `clone.state === 'ok'` and `readable:false`, which is the state the drawn ShareError already depicts. The app must read `clone` from the payload on the FAILURE Result as well as the success one (status.ts:100, :101), because a broken clone is precisely the case that makes status exit 1, and it must never infer clone state from a failing read of its own."

RM-49.title: readReadmeData fails whole on one bad skill folder; ls and search degrade per row
RM-49.delta: `ls` degrades per row (rev N). The team path of `ls` enumerates skills through `skillRecords()` — the same enumerator `search`, `status` and `ls --local` already use — and reads `people/*.json` one file at a time the way `search` does, so one unreadable, unparseable or misnamed `skills/<name>/` folder and one malformed people file each cost exactly that row and one reported line, never the roster, the other skills, or the exit code. The boundary is the `skills/` root itself: if the root cannot be read the verb still fails whole, because a caller must never be shown an empty team when it is looking at an unreadable clone. `LsResult` gains `problems`, naming every skipped source, and `LsSkill` gains `unresolved`, set exactly as `SearchHit.unresolved` is, so a consumer can tell a version that is legitimately an em dash from a row that degraded. Two consequences are deliberate and are behaviour changes on repositories that are healthy today: a folder whose frontmatter `name` disagrees with its directory is now reported and skipped by `ls`, `ls member` and `ls project` — `skillRecords`, the README reader and `findSkill` all already refuse it, so `ls` was advertising skills `install` would not resolve — and a skipped people file no longer hides the roster, though its member's install counts are then absent rather than zero and must be reported as such. The README generator keeps its fail-closed read (§9): a derived artifact that silently drops a skill is worse than one that refuses to regenerate.

TJ-10.title: Project description and icon are drawn everywhere; team.json has neither field
TJ-10.ownerFile: none (a Result field / verb payload — NOT the refused team.json route)
TJ-10.delta: **`team.json projects` entries are `{remotes, skills}` plus whatever the team hand-maintains (rev 13).** The two keys the tool reads and writes are `remotes` and `skills`: row (c) of the §6.0 table permits `publish` to change `projects[].skills` and nothing else inside an entry, and no verb creates or removes a project key at all — `publish --project` refuses a key that is not already present and `team create` scaffolds `projects: {}` — so the `projects` object is hand-maintained on the host through GitHub's own editor (a clone push carrying that change is refused by the pre-push guard, §6.0). Because the schemas preserve unknown fields on write (§5), an entry may carry additional descriptive keys written by hand alongside the rest of the entry — `description` is the one phase 2 renders. They parse, they survive every write (each writer re-serializes the parsed document), and row (c)'s comparison ignores them as long as they do not change, so `publish` is unaffected. They are documentation for humans and for the UI, never a constraint: nothing validates them and no verb writes them. The phase-2 UI renders `projects[<key>].description` read-only when it is present and renders nothing when it is absent; it never stores a description of its own, because a project description is team-wide truth and the UI holds no second source of truth (ledger D20). A project's icon is not a repository field at all: the UI derives it deterministically from the project key, the way it derives a person's initials from `display_name`.
